stories.title: Coravel makes 25 leadership hires in six months through partnership with specialist search firm Metric DCX
stories.summary: Specialist data center search firm has built the ACS and GIP-backed company’s team from C-suite to specialist level across the US, Europe, and Australia, starting ahead of its public launch
stories.title_zh: Coravel通过与专业搜索公司Metric DCX的合作，在六个月内完成25项领导层招聘
stories.content:
When Coravel launched its brand in July, it did so with the backing of ACS Group and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP), part of BlackRock, a 1.7GW development portfolio (1.2GW IT load), and a first major hyperscaler customer agreement covering around 140MW at its Dallas-Fort Worth campus. Delivering on this momentum depends on having experienced leadership in place across every function and region.

Coravel is itself built on partnership, combining ACS’s development, engineering, and construction capability with GIP’s investment expertise, and it offers customers one accountable partner across the data center lifecycle. It has taken the same approach to building its leadership team, working with Metric DCX, a specialist data center executive search firm, as a single partner across every function and region.

Metric DCX began working with the business ahead of its public launch, engaging directly with leaders in each function and running every search from brief to offer with the first appointment made before the company went to market. In total, this partnership has led to 25 appointments from C-suite to specialist level across the US, Europe, and Australia in six months.

Starting early mattered in a market where experienced talent is scarce. More than half of operators responding to Uptime Institute’s 2026 Global Data Center Survey reported difficulty finding qualified candidates, and the shortage has been moving steadily toward senior roles. New entrants compete with established operators for the same leaders and must hire across every function at once.

The team’s make up reflects Coravel’s integrated model, which brings power strategy, site origination, design, construction, capital and operations together for hyperscalers and leading technology companies. This model requires leadership across all of these disciplines at the same time, alongside dedicated leaders in operational technology, physical security and public affairs.

“People are Coravel’s greatest asset, and building an experienced data center team deserves the same rigor as planning for power or capital, because the industry now needs talent at the speed of power,” said Karissa Bussard, chief human resources officer at Coravel. “Culture and the way our people work together are what turn investment and infrastructure into operating data centers for our customers.”

She added: “Coravel was built on the principle of one accountable partner, and we wanted the same from the firm helping us build our team. Metric DCX understood our business and this sector from the outset, and George and the team have operated as a trusted extension of our leadership.”

George Bacon, search partner at Metric DCX, said: “Coravel treated leadership hiring as part of the critical path from the outset, and invested early in functions such as operational technology, security, and community relations, which is where much of the sector’s risk now sits.”

Bacon added that the companies now entering the market are increasingly formed through partnerships of capital, construction, and technology, and that their hiring benefits from the same model.

“When every function has to be filled at once in a market this tight, a search partner embedded with the leadership team from the start can move faster and see further than a series of separate briefs,” he said.

stories.title: Infineon boosts AI sales outlook due to data centre growth plans
stories.summary: (Nov 10): Infineon Technologies AG raised its 2027 data centre sales forecast, signalling confidence that the business will drive growth even as investor concerns mount over the artificial intelligence boom.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Infineon因数据中心增长计划上调AI销售预期
stories.content:
The German chipmaker sees data centre sales growing to around €4 billion (US$4.5 billion) in the year that ends in September, it said in a statement on Tuesday. Previously, Infineon forecast AI data centre power solutions would make €2.5 billion in the period. It also makes about €500 million annually from traditional data centres, and the new figure comprises both segments.

“We expect a significant increase in revenue and profitability in fiscal year 2027,” chief executive officer Jochen Hanebeck said in the statement, adding power chips for data centres and electromobility would be among the growth drivers.

Concerns about a possible AI bubble have driven a steep selloff in companies from chipmakers to so-called neoclouds. Infineon’s shares have declined by 45% from a peak in June. Demand for data centre chips has helped Infineon and peers such as STMicroelectronics NV compensate for slow revenue recovery from the struggling automotive sector.

Infineon is the only one among European chipmakers to give a full year forecast. The company tends to guide cautiously and then adjust estimates as visibility improves, according to JPMorgan analysts including Sandeep Deshpande. JPMorgan had expected Infineon to guide for 2027 data center revenue, including CPU and other non-AI accelerator-related power revenue, of between €3.5 billion and €4 billion.

As the buildout of data centers around the world accelerated, demand for Infineon’s chips to control power soared. Those chips can support advanced processors such as those from Nvidia Corp that are fuelling the AI boom.

However, a punishing post-US election selloff has rippled across the industry. Some potential investors in Anthropic PBC, which can begin formal marketing of its initial public offering as soon as Tuesday, discussed a valuation ranging from about US$1.1 trillion to US$1.3 trillion, well below where talks had been focused just a month ago, *Bloomberg News* reported last week.

Infineon’s fiscal 2026 revenue was €16.35 billion, matching analysts’ estimates, according to data compiled by *Bloomberg*. The company sees sales growing to about €20 billion in the current year. The board will propose increasing the 2026 dividend by three cents to €0.38.

Infineon said its adjusted gross margin will be in the mid-to-high forties percentage range in the period and it plans investments of €3 billion to €3.5 billion. Adjusted gross margin was 43.1% in fiscal 2026.

The main areas of investment will be equipment for the ramp-up of production at Infineon’s Dresden site in Germany, the expansion of silicon carbide capacities in Malaysia, and the start of gallium nitride manufacturing on 300-millimetre wafers in the Austrian town of Villach.

Infineon is also considering setting up wafer fabrication in Thailand, although such a move is unlikely in the next three years. In September, Infineon announced it will sell parts of its memory business to focus on its core activities and more dynamic parts of its portfolio.

stories.title: EPG tops out US$120 million factory for modular data centers
stories.summary: EPG Modular Data Center has topped out its $120 million manufacturing facility in Senai Airport City, Johor, establishing one of the largest single-site modular data center production bases globally by capacity. The Malaysia Free Industrial Zone factory will supply prefabricated data center infrastructure to meet accelerating APAC demand.
stories.why_it_matters: EPG's factory investment validates modular construction as a mainstream delivery method for APAC data centers, compressing deployment timelines from years to months for power-constrained markets. The facility strengthens Malaysia's position in the data center supply chain beyond colocation hosting, creating local manufacturing expertise that could attract complementary industries like precision cooling and power distribution equipment.
stories.title_zh: EPG为模块化数据中心封顶1.2亿美元工厂
stories.summary_zh: EPG Modular Data Center已为其位于Johor Senai Airport City的1.2亿美元制造工厂举行封顶仪式，按产能建立了全球最大的单site modular data center生产基地之一。这家马来西亚Free Industrial Zone工厂将供应prefabricated data center基础设施，以满足加速增长的亚太需求。
stories.why_zh: EPG的工厂投资验证了modular construction作为亚太地区data center主流交付方法的地位，将电力受限市场的部署时间从数年压缩到数月。该设施加强了马来西亚在data center供应链中超越colocation hosting的地位，创造了可能吸引精密冷却和电力分配设备等互补行业的本地制造专业知识。
stories.content:
Asia-based prefabricated modular data center infrastructure provider EPG Modular Data Center last Friday topped out its US$120 million Malaysia FIZ (Free Industrial Zone) Factory in Senai Airport City (SAC), Johor. The facility is among the largest single-site data center module manufacturing bases in the modular data center (MDC) sector by production capacity, the firm says in a press release.

In modular construction, components of a building or system are built in a factory before being shipped out to the construction site to be assembled. The Johor site has the advantage of being closer to its Southeast Asian customers enabling faster response.

Spanning 107,450 square meters, including 70,000 sqm of production space, the factory is expected to be completed in 1Q 2027. The master plan comprises five buildings for sheet metal production, power transfer unit (PTU) products, diesel generator manufacturing, final assembly, and R&D and office functions. It will integrate advanced automation equipment, intelligent control systems and automated welding technology, achieving an expected automation rate of at least 80 pe cent.

By consolidating production of MDC shelters and critical power equipment in Malaysia, EPG is building capacity closer to regional customers.

“The FIZ Factory marks an important step in bringing EPG’s manufacturing capabilities closer to customers and the markets we serve,” said Alick Wan, EPG’s founder and chairman. “By combining advanced manufacturing with strong local partnerships, we are building a responsive base in Malaysia and a model that can evolve with customer needs in other markets.”

It is expected to employ more than 800 people locally once fully operational.

stories.title: Schneider Electric opens regional centre to build technical skills
stories.summary: French energy management and automation company Schneider Electric has opened a regional training centre in an attempt to help workers keep pace with technological advances in data centres and other industries across Asia-Pacific.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Schneider Electric开设区域中心以培养技术技能
stories.content:
PETALING JAYA (Nov 10): French energy management and automation company Schneider Electric has opened a regional training centre in an attempt to help workers keep pace with technological advances in data centres and other industries across Asia-Pacific.

The 18,500 sq ft facility in Petaling Jaya has the capacity to train more than 550 participants annually from 15 Asia-Pacific countries.

Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Datuk Chang Lih Kang said practical training was increasingly important as investment in artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductor manufacturing, smart factories and renewable energy raised demand for skilled workers.

He warned that engineers, technicians and young technical and vocational education and training (TVET) graduates risked being left behind as technology advanced.

“In the first half of 2026, Malaysia recorded more than RM200 billion in approved investments, including RM95 billion in data centres and cloud infrastructure, particularly in Selangor and Johor,” he said at the launch.

“Without equipping our engineers, technicians, and young TVET talents with practical, industry-relevant skills, we risk leaving our workforce behind while technology advances.”

Chang said the centre could help turn national innovation policies into economic gains by developing workers with industry-relevant skills, supporting knowledge and technology transfer, and connecting local start-ups with industrial expertise.

With the right tools and training, Malaysians could compete internationally and take on roles developing, operating and leading technologies across the region, he added.

The opening also builds on France–Malaysia cooperation in technology, innovation and talent development as the countries approach 70 years of diplomatic relations. French ambassador to Malaysia Marc Abensour said the centre would bring international expertise together with local experience, allowing engineers and technicians from different markets to exchange knowledge and collaborate.

“French companies are not here as short-term visitors. They are here as long-term partners, growing alongside the nation and investing in its future,” he said.

Schneider Electric Malaysia country president Eugene Quah said Malaysia was chosen for its talent, strategic location, growing digital economy and government commitment to skills development.

He said linking the training academy with the company’s service teams would allow problems encountered at customers’ facilities to be incorporated into training.

“That means what we learn from customers shapes our training, and what we teach helps solve the issues they face,” he said.

Training will be offered to Schneider Electric employees, customers, partners and contractors to improve their ability to install, operate and maintain energy and automation systems.

Courses will cover low- and medium-voltage electrical distribution equipment, including circuit breakers and transformers, as well as backup power supplies and battery systems. Other training will focus on energy management, industrial automation and digital tools for monitoring data centre operations.

Trainees will work with functioning equipment to practise identifying faults and learn how electrical supplies, backup power and monitoring systems work together.

stories.summary: TOKYO (Nov 10): Japan's SoftBank Group said on Tuesday that it had swung to a second-quarter net loss of US$7 billion, hit hard by hefty buildout costs for data centres in the US and increases in financing payments.

stories.title_zh: SoftBank因美国数据中心冲击及融资成本录得70亿美元季度亏损
stories.content:
TOKYO (Nov 10): Japan's SoftBank Group said on Tuesday that it had swung to a second-quarter net loss of US$7 billion, hit hard by hefty buildout costs for data centres in the US and increases in financing payments.

The result will likely intensify questions about how well the tech investment giant can weather setbacks currently buffeting the AI sector, given founder Masayoshi Son's big bets on data centres and the company's US$64.6 billion purchase of a 13% stake in ChatGPT maker OpenAI.

SoftBank said it recorded a US$3.7 billion loss due to a subsidiary's advance payments for power generation equipment to be used in AI data centre projects in the US including Pike County, Ohio. Those plans were later revised. It is, however, entitled to rebates of up to US$2.1 billion on future purchases.

Its financing costs also more than doubled to 462 billion yen (US$2.9 billion) in the quarter.

The 1.1 trillion yen net loss for the July-September quarter compares with a 2.5 trillion yen profit in the same period a year earlier when it logged a huge investment gain on an increase in the value of its stake in OpenAI.

SoftBank's earnings are volatile and difficult to predict. Forecasts from three analysts polled by LSEG had ranged from a profit of 233 billion yen to a loss of 113 billion yen.

The Democratic Party's sweeping success in US midterm elections last week heightened expectations of regulatory scrutiny, amplifying concerns that had been growing among investors about returns for the AI industry.

Though SoftBank's shares surged 14% on Tuesday ahead of the results, they have, like other AI stocks, been battered by the cooling investor sentiment, almost halving in value since the start of June.

The sector was further rocked this week by the news that the FBI is looking at Jensen Huang, Nvidia's CEO and the face of the AI boom, after his affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. SoftBank was a major investor in the AI chipmaker in the past but no longer holds a stake.

SoftBank's heavy borrowing at sometimes eye-popping yields has been a concern for some investors.

During the quarter, SoftBank's borrowing included an US$11.87 billion term loan, a US$10 billion dollar-denominated corporate bond and a one trillion yen-denominated corporate bond.

SoftBank also increased the margin loan on its stake in chipmaker Arm by US$5 billion to roughly US$25 billion.

While SoftBank's stake in TikTok maker ByteDance generated an investment gain of US$1.3 billion during the quarter, share prices of major public portfolio companies such as Coupang and Grab declined.

stories.title: Malaysia's limited data centre locations, rising costs could weigh on competitiveness
stories.summary: Industry participants warn that Malaysia's restricted geographic options for data center development and escalating operational expenses may undermine its competitive position against emerging alternatives in Thailand and Indonesia. The concentration of projects in Johor and limited power infrastructure elsewhere create bottlenecks for sustained growth.
stories.why_it_matters: Malaysia's data center boom faces a maturity test as first-mover advantages in Johor give way to land scarcity and grid constraints, while rival markets offer fresher development corridors and government incentives. Operators with pan-ASEAN strategies—particularly STT GDC, AirTrunk and Chinese hyperscalers—may rebalance investment toward Bangkok, Jakarta and emerging Indonesian markets, diversifying APAC's data center geography beyond the Singapore-Johor corridor.

stories.summary_zh: 行业参与者警告称，马来西亚有限的data center开发地理选择和不断上升的运营成本可能削弱其相对于泰国和印尼新兴替代方案的竞争地位。项目在Johor的集中以及其他地区有限的电力基础设施为持续增长创造了瓶颈。

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 10): Malaysia’s relatively limited choice of locations for data centre development, coupled with rising operating costs, could affect its ability to compete with regional markets such as Thailand and Indonesia, industry players said.

Speaking at Bursa Malaysia’s Sectorial Series, *Powering the AI Era — Watt Next?*, IVPS Malaysia (Cushman & Wakefield) managing director and country manager Tiffany Goh said Malaysia’s data centre clusters were relatively concentrated compared to regional peers, with the majority located in Johor.

She noted that Thailand offered developers more options in terms of power providers and Indonesia had a wider geographical spread of potential sites.

Malaysia’s constraints include the availability of power and water, as well as the distance between suitable locations, she said.

Greater Kuala Lumpur remains attractive because of its existing infrastructure while Johor continues to be another key data centre hub, said Isaac Goh, general manager of data centre architecture and delivery of TM Global — the wholesale domestic and international business arm of Telekom Malaysia Bhd (KL:TM).

Northern states could also offer opportunities, although latency, which is the time taken for data to travel between locations, may be a consideration that may prove to be an obstacle for certain workloads, he said.

Isaac said latency of between seven and nine milliseconds could be suitable for some applications, including AI training, but AI inference may require a lower range of about five to six milliseconds.

The comments were made during a panel discussion titled *Malaysia’s Data Centre Boom: Sustaining Growth in the Next Phase*, which was moderated by Macquarie utilities and construction analyst Colin Lee.

(Nov 10): Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co posted a 60% increase in monthly sales, reflecting the company’s central role in a global AI infrastructure build-out.

The go-to chipmaker for Nvidia Corp and Apple Inc reported October revenue of NT$586.9 billion (RM72.39 billion). That pace was up from around 51% for the September quarter. Analysts on average are projecting 63% growth for the year’s final three months.

Taiwan’s largest company last month delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook, sustaining a torrid pace of growth in the post-ChatGPT era. Yet investors continue to grapple with the longer-term outlook for AI demand, given the rising cost of financing expensive and resource-hungry data centres. TSMC’s shares have gyrated alongside the rest of the tech sector, buffeted by fears that the Democrats’ sweep of Congress in the US midterms may lead to tougher oversight of the artificial intelligence sector.

TSMC — a key barometer for the industry because it makes chips for a broad swathe of tech players — is betting on a fundamental shift. It is trying to build and furnish about 20 factories at home and overseas, an unprecedented pace for a company that typically works on four or five new buildings simultaneously.

CEO C C Wei has stressed, though, that it remains in prudent expansion mode, exploring a new manufacturing site in Texas while discussing a potential tie-up with Elon Musk’s Terafab chipmaking endeavour.

The company has so far managed to accelerate sales growth and ramped up capacity expansion. The company reiterated its capital expenditures will reach as much as US$64 billion (RM259.36 billion), a record, this year.

stories.title: AI data centers demand power grid overhaul, says Huawei executive
stories.summary: Huawei executive He Bo described AI data centers as evolving into 'token factories' where daily token usage for models like ByteDance's Doubao surged 1,500-fold within a year. These facilities now exhibit extreme power volatility, with AI clusters consuming up to 200% more electricity during intensive training and inference phases compared to baseline operations.
stories.why_it_matters: Grid operators and data center designers must fundamentally rethink power architecture for AI workloads, moving from steady-state assumptions to dynamic load management. This volatility challenge creates openings for battery storage, fuel cells and smart grid integration vendors, while raising questions about whether traditional utility contracts can accommodate such unpredictable demand patterns.
stories.title_zh: 华为高管称AI数据中心需要电网改造
stories.summary_zh: 华为高管He Bo将AI data center描述为正在演变为"token工厂"，其中ByteDance的Doubao等模型的日token使用量在一年内激增1500倍。这些设施现在表现出极端的电力波动性，AI集群在密集training和inference阶段的电力消耗比基线运营高出多达200%。
stories.why_zh: 电网运营商和data center设计师必须从根本上为AI工作负载重新思考电力架构，从稳态假设转向动态负载管理。这种波动性挑战为电池储能、燃料电池和智能电网集成供应商创造了机会，同时引发了关于传统电力合同能否适应如此不可预测的需求模式的问题。
stories.content:
Data centers now operate as "token factories" for artificial intelligence (AI) output, a significant shift from their traditional role supporting enterprise applications and cloud services. This transformation is driven by exponential growth in token usage, with ByteDance's Doubao model experiencing a 1,500-fold surge in daily token usage in one year, according to He Bo, Vice President of Huawei Digital Power.AI clusters exhibit power draw fluctuations of up to 200 per cent during training and inference, unlike the stable consumption of conventional data centers, He Bo noted. These swings occur across multiple timescales, from milliseconds at the chip level to hours for job scheduling.The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects global data center electricity consumption will double by 2030 from 2024 levels. Securing sufficient power is one challenge, but grid stability is another, especially as Asia Pacific grids become electrically weaker with increased renewable energy integration, He Bo stated.Huawei proposes a "3+1" strategy encompassing watt, heat, bit, and construction innovation to address these challenges. The company's MIMO architecture, featuring a grid-forming energy router, is designed to stabilise power from diverse inputs like utilities, renewables, batteries, and backup generators.Layered energy storage systems, using capacitors, supercapacitors, and grid-forming batteries, are needed to manage power fluctuations at different speeds. Liquid cooling has become essential for high-density racks, with AI-driven thermal management shifting operations from reactive to predictive, He Bo added. Grid strength, power access, and renewable energy availability will ultimately determine the pace of AI data center construction across markets.

stories.title: Japan's Rapidus is said likely to miss mass production deadline
stories.summary: Japanese government-backed startup Rapidus Corp has fallen behind schedule on its high-stakes pledge to mass produce cutting-edge chips by March 2028 and may no longer be able to make that deadline.

stories.title_zh: 日本Rapidus据称可能错过大规模生产截止日期
stories.content:
(Nov 10): Japanese government-backed startup Rapidus Corp has fallen behind schedule on its high-stakes pledge to mass produce cutting-edge chips by March 2028 and may no longer be able to make that deadline.

The startup, which has received billions of dollars’ worth of public funds, has yet to successfully produce a key type of advanced memory that is an essential component of all processors, people familiar with the matter said. Rapidus has yet to produce functioning static random access memory cells, or SRAM, a critical step that needed to be completed by the summer to manufacture 2nm chips in time, they said.

Engineers are under intense pressure to pick up the pace but the failure to meet that technological milestone means the company is at least months behind schedule, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public.

A significant delay may jeopardise public support for Rapidus, widely viewed as a long-shot attempt to build a top-tier foundry from scratch and lower Japan’s advanced chip reliance on Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Dust and particle control within the cleanroom remains another issue the company is working to resolve, the people said.

The government has so far officially earmarked more than ¥2 trillion (RM51 billion) in state funding to Rapidus. Severe technological issues could also push back Rapidus’s goal of going public by 2032.

“Rapidus continues to devote its full efforts toward the start of mass production in the second half of fiscal 2027,” a spokesperson said in an email. The company declined to provide details about its technological development, which it said is confidential. In September, a panel of outside experts commissioned by a government agency reported the company’s development is progressing, it said.

Last month, Rapidus chairman Tetsuro Higashi said the venture was on track for mass production as scheduled, without elaborating.

Advanced logic chips require hundreds of millions of embedded SRAM cells. Manufacturers need to reproduce each of these cells, including their transistors, at atomic-scale precision to prevent operational failures and ensure stable data retention. At the nanometre scale, even a minor microscopic deviation can cause debilitating chip failures.

Rapidus will continue to pursue 2nm manufacturing and may ultimately succeed after some years’ delay, the people said. Rapidus seeks to compete against Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, which is building facilities in the US, Intel Corp and Samsung Electronics Co. All are racing to develop manufacturing processes and meet artificial intelligence service providers’ voracious demand for increasingly powerful chips.

After launching its pilot production line at its factory in Hokkaido, northern Japan, Rapidus said in July last year that it successfully manufactured functioning transistors — an early step toward making cutting-edge chips. Since then, technological progress has consisted mainly of process design kit releases.

Last month, Economy Minister Ryosei Akazawa said the government was ready to continue supporting Rapidus until the venture becomes financially viable, given the importance of cutting-edge chips for Japan’s economic security. Since Rapidus’ creation in 2022, TSMC has built a plant in southern Japan, with plans to build another factory that will manufacture 3nm chips.

In September, independent director Yoshimitsu Kobayashi told *Bloomberg News* that Rapidus is targeting mass production with a yield of at least 80%, or four out of every five chips produced. CEO Atsuyoshi Koike, who has floated plans to build two additional factories in Hokkaido and a plant on the moon, and representative director Atsuo Shimizu have said that Kobayashi’s definition is not shared by all executives.

stories.title: China's trade surplus soars past US$1 trillion as AI boom powers exports
stories.summary: Exports rose sharply by 35.2% in October from the same month last year
stories.title_zh: AI热潮推动出口，中国贸易顺差突破1万亿美元
stories.content:
Exports rose sharply by 35.2% in October from the same month last year

\[BEIJING\] China’s trade surplus surged past US$1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.

The figures highlight Beijing’s growing reliance on overseas demand to support an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump.

But while the global AI investment boom is expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027, it risks deepening domestic imbalances and fuelling trade frictions with partners including the European Union.

Exports rose sharply by 35.2 per cent in October from the same month last year in US dollar terms, customs data showed on Tuesday (Nov 10), only a touch slower than the 36.3 per cent surge in September, but ahead of economists’ forecast for an increase of 33.5 per cent.

That helped lift China’s trade surplus to US$1.04 trillion in the first 10 months, topping US$1 trillion for a second consecutive year and reaching the milestone a month earlier than in 2025.

The swelling surplus could fuel further tensions with the European Union, where leaders have called for more trade curbs with China after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc over the next few years.

Because the measures have yet to take effect, factories are expected to bring forward shipments, bolstering exports in the near term.

China on Monday officially announced the extension of a trade truce with Washington due to expire on Nov 10 by two months, but said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of their agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.

“The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets,” said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.

Against that backdrop, imports rose 41.6 per cent in October from a year earlier, beating the median forecast for a 32 per cent increase in the Reuters poll and accelerating from the 31 per cent growth in September.

China’s trade surplus with the US dipped slightly to US$32.71 billion in October from US$34.01 billion the previous month, but the larger gap remains a point of friction between the two economic superpowers.

Oil imports fell 13.3 per cent from a year earlier, though shipments reached their highest level since March as buyers sought supplies after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted Middle East flows.

The trade data comes ahead of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time this year, putting trade frictions and tariff policy squarely in focus.

Following a September summit between Xi and Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods

### Headwinds and uncertainties

One big worry for Beijing is that consumers remain reluctant to spend, constrained by a property market downturn that has battered household wealth and dented confidence in the economic outlook.

Sluggish demand at home has pushed Chinese automakers to seek sales in overseas markets. China’s car exports maintained a solid pace of growth in October, while domestic vehicle sales recorded a 12th straight month of declines, separate data released by an industry association showed.

Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China’s economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand.

Much of the strength in exports this year has been fuelled by a global push to expand AI infrastructure.

“The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last,” Macquarie analysts wrote. They expect China’s exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027. REUTERS

stories.title: Power is the new blueprint for the AI data center
stories.summary: Data centers used to exist solely for enterprise applications and the cloud. Today, they are increasingly used to produce tokens, the unit in which AI output is generated and billed. stories.title_zh: Power is the new blueprint for the AI data center
stories.content:
Data centers used to exist solely for enterprise applications and the cloud. Today, they are increasingly used to produce tokens, the unit in which AI output is generated and billed. And the numbers suggest a “token factory” era is already here. According to Huawei’s He Bo, Vice President of Huawei Digital Power, daily token usage of ByteDance’s Doubao model alone grew roughly 1,500-fold in the year to June.

This has consequences, because token factories are a very different kind of load. The power draw of an AI cluster can fluctuate by up to 200% amid training and inference runs, says He, unlike a typical data center that draws a steady amount of power around the clock.

#### **Stable power is crucial** 

And such swings are happening more often, as token processing volumes surge. In China alone, volume grew roughly 2,500-fold in the last two years, according to Huawei’s figures. Overall electricity consumption is climbing steeply too, with the International Energy Agency (IEA) expecting global data center electricity consumption to double from 2024 levels by 2030. Yet securing enough power is only half the problem.

The other half is whether the grid can tolerate how that power is used. The fluctuations happen on several fronts simultaneously, says He. At the chip level, power draw changes within milliseconds, while swings in the data hall happen over minutes. Zoom out further, and consumption can rise and fall over hours as new jobs get scheduled. The problem? No single piece of equipment is designed to handle all of that.

The power grids themselves are also changing. As renewable energy displaces conventional power generation across Asia Pacific, grids are becoming electrically weaker, with lower short-circuit ratios that make them more prone to voltage swings and oscillation, says He. And as facilities scale into the gigawatts, grids are now far less able to absorb disturbances than they once were.

Getting enough power is just the start. Power densities inside the building keep rising with each iteration of AI hardware, and the heat has to be removed just as quickly. Crucially, the data center can no longer be a passive load. It is no longer enough to simply ride through voltage and frequency events. In some cases, the facility will be expected to play a part to help the grid recover from them.

#### **From the grid to the chip** 

The fix, according to He, lies in looking at the whole facility rather than its parts. A more efficient UPS or a better CDU helps, but the bigger gains come from rethinking the entire electricity pathway through the facility. His framework for this is what Huawei calls\[z1.1\] its “3+1” Strategy, for watt innovation, heat innovation, and bit innovation, as well as construction\[z2.1\] innovation using prefabrication.

Take power first. The grid to chip chain must get shorter and lose fewer watts along the way. Yet that chain is getting more complicated. Utility power, renewables, batteries and backup generators all feed in, while AC and several flavors of DC will coexist on the server side for years. Huawei’s answer is an architecture it calls MIMO, built around a grid-forming energy router that takes in multiple energy inputs and turns them into stable power. This allows a single power foundation to serve every output type.

The same thinking applies to energy storage, which should be layered according to how fast the swings are. Capacitors on the board absorb the fastest ones, supercapacitors and short-duration lithium batteries handle the data hall, and grid-forming battery systems smooth things out at the campus level, so each layer hands off to the next.

Cooling must keep up with density, too. Liquid cooling has gone from an option to a necessity. But at above 100kW per rack, thermal inertia is so low that a cooling failure may leave operators about a minute to respond, says He. The points of failure multiply as well, since the coolant now runs through the server. His fix is AI-driven thermal management that flags minor leaks and declining coolant quality before they become faults, so that operations shift from reacting to problems to predicting them.

#### **Grid strength will decide who builds first** 

All of which raises the question of whether the current wave of data center construction across Asia Pacific is sustainable, or a temporary bubble. He is firmly in the first camp. Token demand is growing exponentially, and gigawatt-scale AI data centers are moving from a small handful of projects to routine deployments. In his view, this is a long investment cycle driven by a structural shift in computing.

But it will not unfold evenly. Access to power, grid connection capacity, renewable energy availability and construction speed differ widely across markets. And those factors will ultimately decide how fast each market moves. In other words, grid conditions do not just determine how stable a facility is once built. They determine when it gets built at all; some markets will see protracted development over years while others move far quicker.

Huawei’s pitch is breadth. On the energy side, it builds everything from generation and grid equipment to storage, power supply and thermal management. It also makes the chips, the models and the applications that run on them. That lets the company design and simulate the whole system together, He argues, instead of assembling parts from different vendors.

“We are not simply combining UPS systems, lithium batteries, and liquid cooling equipment,” he summed up. In the token factory, power is where the design starts, because the ultimate limit of compute is electricity.

stories.title_zh: 部长称PETRONAS可用天然气为数据中心供电，按市场价锁定长期买家
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 10): PETRONAS could tap into the massive power demand from data centres by supplying gas for dedicated power generation, a minister said on Tuesday.

If successful, the national oil-and-gas company officially known as Petroliam Nasional Bhd may secure longer-term customers at market prices, rather than provide subsidised energy to data centres, said Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.

The boom in data centres presented an opportunity for Malaysia's gas industry to develop an additional domestic market, he said.

Johari was delivering his keynote address at Bursa Malaysia's *Sectoral Series: Powering the AI Era — Watt Next?* The remarks come as a wave of energy-intensive data centres has been surging across Malaysia amid a global boom in artificial intelligence.

Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA), the country’s national electric utility firm, is now supplying power to 36 data centres with dozens more in the pipeline.

Malaysia could explore supplying gas to data centres through dedicated power generation, alongside other energy sources such as solar, rather than relying solely on electricity from the national grid, Johari said.

He highlighted the potential to redirect some of the country's gas resources towards domestic power generation, subject to existing export commitments and domestic energy requirements.

Longer-term supply arrangements could provide energy producers with greater certainty over demand, while allowing data centre operators to secure the power needed for their operations, Johari noted.

Gas resources are finite and any supply arrangements would need to be priced transparently, taking into account market conditions and existing commitments, Johari said, stressing that existing long-term export contracts and infrastructure policy will be honoured in the meantime.

The growing electricity requirements of data centres could also support investment in other parts of the energy sector, including power generation, battery energy storage and grid infrastructure, he added.

Malaysia is seeking to develop the infrastructure needed to support the country's digital economy while ensuring that the investments also create opportunities for the domestic energy industry and wider supply chain.

The government wants data centre investors to bear the cost of transmission upgrades required by their projects rather than pass it on to the locals. Operators would also be charged for capacity committed even if they did not fully use it, to prevent the allocations from being tied up without compensation.

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 10): The Democratic sweep of both US congressional chambers in the midterm elections has weighed on technology stocks globally, but analysts said Malaysian tech faces a sentiment and valuation dip rather than an earnings hit.

MBSB Research said a blanket negative view of Malaysian technology would be "inappropriate", since impact depends on each company's exposure.

The exposure, it said, ranges from AI servers and data-centre equipment to semiconductor testing, consumer electronics, capital-equipment orders, customer concentration and balance-sheet strength.

"Tighter regulation does not remove the physical requirements of AI. AI still requires electricity, grid connections, buildings, cooling systems, water treatment, fibre networks, cybersecurity and backup power. Even a more regulated industry must continue investing in secure and efficient infrastructure," said the house in a note on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Kenanga Investment Bank said the post-US midterm unease has dragged Malaysian tech names down by sentiment, and that for the sector, it foresees "a sentiment and valuations dip rather than earnings" from delayed data-centre rollout.

Kenanga views any shift of data-centre development outside the US — such as Meta eyeing overseas expansion — as "a modest positive for Malaysia," likely extending the visibility of the local data-centre play rather than accelerating demand.

It also noted Google's commitment to spend US$15 billion in Malaysia over 2027/2028.

MBSB said the near-term Malaysian transmission is primarily through sentiment, with Bursa Malaysia technology companies exposed to Nasdaq and semiconductor valuations, and warned that "US policy risk becomes Malaysian valuation risk before it becomes Malaysian earnings risk".

MBSB's preferred durable exposure is in the physical infrastructure surrounding data centres, including Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA), YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR), Gamuda (KL:GAMUDA), Sunway Construction Group Bhd (KL:SUNCON), IJM Corporation (KL:IJM), CelcomDigi Bhd (KL:CBD) and Maxis Bhd (KL:MAXIS).

Kenanga cautioned that local barriers are also tightening, with 24 applications for approval on hold pending power and water checks, and that 12.3GW of energy capacity had been approved for data centres as of August, with maximum sector demand projected to reach 8.39GW by 2030.

Kenanga said YTL Power and property names are "unduly discounted" for their data-centre prospects — YTL Power's last close of RM5.01 implies only 600MW of its pipeline is being credited versus its 1.2GW forecast.

Meanwhile, data-centre valuations account for 7%–14% of target prices for Sime Darby Property Bhd (KL:SIMEPROP), EcoWorld Development Group Bhd (KL:ECOWLD) and Mah Sing Group Bhd (KL:MAHSING).

It likes Tenaga Nasional, seeing the discount implied by skepticism over the IBR mechanism as excessive, and Kee Ming Group Bhd (KL:KEEMING) as a beneficiary of data-centre-related electrical works, with Sunway Construction as its preferred pure-play data-centre exposure.

On technology, Kenanga remains positive on Nationgate Holdings Bhd (KL:NATGATE) and Ambest Group (KL:AMBEST) and likes Kelington Group Bhd (KL:KGB) for its secured 2027/2028 revenue, but said it does not yet see urgency for bargain hunting for tech names sector-wide.

Both houses expect Malaysian equities to remain supported by resilient domestic growth, healthy corporate earnings and continued infrastructure and data centre investment.

MBSB kept its preliminary end-2027 FBM KLCI target at 1,850 points, based on forecast index earnings of 120.1 points (6.6% growth) and a forward PER of 15.4 times.

Both houses favour a balanced approach — utilities, construction, telecommunications, healthcare and essential consumption alongside selective technology.

MBSB noted further that lower oil prices would provide the necessary market confirmation for its 1,850-point target.

stories.title: Data centre liquid cooling needs standardised commissioning
stories.summary: Ecolab Corporate Scientist Bob Walicki identified significant gaps between liquid cooling commissioning practices and rapidly advancing GPU densities in modern AI data centers. Inconsistent standards for validating liquid cooling loop performance risk thermal degradation and threaten the reliability of high-value AI computing infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: The commissioning gap creates immediate operational risk for operators deploying Nvidia H100/H200 and future GPU generations, where thermal failures can destroy millions in hardware within minutes. Industry bodies like ASHRAE and Uptime Institute face pressure to rapidly standardize liquid cooling acceptance protocols, while commissioning service providers gain a new specialized market as traditional air-cooled expertise becomes obsolete for AI workloads.
stories.title_zh: 数据中心液冷需要标准化调试
stories.summary_zh: Ecolab企业科学家Bob Walicki指出现代AI data center中liquid cooling commissioning practices与快速发展的GPU密度之间存在显著差距。验证liquid cooling loop性能的不一致标准可能导致热性能下降，并威胁高价值AI计算基础设施的可靠性。
stories.why_zh: 这一commissioning差距为部署Nvidia H100/H200及未来GPU generation的运营商创造了即时运营风险，热故障可能在数分钟内摧毁数百万美元的硬件。ASHRAE和Uptime Institute等行业机构面临快速标准化liquid cooling acceptance protocols的压力，同时commissioning服务提供商获得了一个新的专业市场，因为传统的air-cooled专业知识对于AI工作负载已变得过时。
stories.content:
The commissioning of data centre liquid cooling systems requires standardisation as GPU densities rise, according to Bob Walicki, Corporate Scientist at Ecolab.Walicki noted that direct-to-chip (D2C) liquid cooling has scaled faster than the commissioning practices supporting it. This has led to varied acceptance criteria across sites, contractors and shifts, creating risks for expensive GPU clusters used in AI training and inference. Organisations including the Open Compute Project (OCP) and ASHRAE have issued guidance for pre-commissioning and fluid quality in liquid-cooled IT equipment.
### Commissioning Challenges

Microchannels within cold plates, often measured in microns, are highly susceptible to debris like weld slag, thread sealant, construction dust and biofilm. These contaminants can degrade thermal performance long before causing outright failure. Ecolab’s global coolant testing across operating data centres showed approximately 32 per cent of glycol samples fell outside OCP and ASHRAE specifications.Addressing these issues requires documented sequencing, not new technology. A written pre-commissioning plan should specify make-up water quality, cleaning chemistry compatible with system metallurgy and elastomers, and wastewater disposal. Flushing should be staged, starting with coarse filtration and moving to fine filtration once bulk contamination is removed. Flow velocity during flushing is crucial, typically 0.9-1.5 m/s, to keep sediment suspended. The period between hydrotest and active circulation should be hours, not days, to prevent biofilm and sediment build-up.
### Monitoring and Handover

Instrumentation, including calibrated flow meters, pressure gauges, and inline conductivity, pH and turbidity monitoring, should be in place before flushing begins. This provides a baseline for auditing system performance over its lifespan. This baseline should also mark the handover from commissioning to operations, allowing continuous telemetry to track coolant chemistry, particulate levels and flow performance. Operators should insist on written commissioning plans, detailed records of flushing, matched cleaning chemistry and persistent instrumentation for ongoing monitoring.

stories.title: Renewable developers must optimise data center grid connections
stories.summary: Renewable energy developers are increasingly interfacing with data centers, which drive exponential load growth on the grid. They must navigate complex interconnection requirements for both generation assets and large loads.
stories.title_zh: 可再生能源开发商必须优化数据中心电网连接
stories.content:
Renewable energy developers are increasingly interfacing with data centers, which are driving exponential load growth on the grid. These developers are well-positioned to meet this demand, often leveraging existing projects or development pipelines.The relationship between renewables and data centers is complex. Renewables alone do not provide firm, standalone power to a data center. Renewable projects are permitted, financed, and interconnected as generation assets, while data centers are sited and interconnected as large loads. This difference affects the end-to-end review process.
### Optimising Interconnection and Design

Renewable developers need to understand and optimise both generation and large load interconnection requirements. This includes navigating grid-stability upgrades, dynamic modeling, ride-through, and voltage support. Developers with strong transmission and interconnection positions for both load and generation have a structural advantage.Projects should be designed as power campuses, not standalone renewable plants. Developers should plan for substations, future load growth, and co-located thermal, renewable, and storage infrastructure on the same site. Planning for co-location upfront, including permitting, is materially cheaper than retrofitting a site later.
### Integrating Firm Power Solutions

Renewable generation paired with energy storage is not enough to support a large data center's reliability needs, particularly when islanded. A 1-GW islanded site lacks an external grid reference for voltage or frequency. Artificial intelligence (AI) training load ramps of 100 MW to 200 MW per minute can create inherent instability.For a data center project to ride through a power disturbance, it needs to pair renewables and storage with firm, synchronous generation and voltage-stabilising equipment. This ensures all system components, including the uninterruptible power supply (UPS), are prepared for power fluctuations. Grid-forming battery energy storage systems (BESS) offer flexibility for reliability, power quality, and load swings, but are insufficient on their own to power a data center at scale.
### Behind-the-Meter and Operational Planning

More developers are turning to behind-the-meter (BTM) generation to power data centers faster, as utility connection timelines stretch. BTM generation can serve as a bridge until a full interconnection is secured. Some regions, like PJM, formalise this path with expedited load interconnection programmes.Developers should plan for multiple operating scenarios from the outset. A project might start as an islanded microgrid, move through a bridge power phase, and then land on a full utility interconnection. Choosing bridge-phase equipment that can transition to permanent operation avoids expensive redesigns and stranded equipment later.Projects should also design for demand response and future grid services. Utilities increasingly make demand response participation a condition of interconnection. Strong projects preserve the flexibility to reduce load, support the grid, or export power when conditions warrant. Jonathan Howie, a senior managing consultant at Ramboll, noted that success comes from integrating generation, storage, interconnection, and reliability into a single power strategy.

stories.title: Synopsys joins Singapore tropical data centre testbed
stories.summary: The partnership aims to curb soaring cooling costs for AI-ready data centres in humid climates, where energy use can reach 40%.
stories.title_zh: Synopsys加入Singapore tropical data centre testbed
stories.content:
Tue, 10th Nov 2026 (Today)
Synopsys has joined the Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed 2.0 consortium, led by the National University of Singapore. The collaboration focuses on data centre cooling and digital modelling for tropical conditions.

Hosted by the university's College of Design and Engineering, the consortium brings together industry and academic researchers working on infrastructure for AI and high-performance computing systems. The work will connect engineering simulation, AI-assisted design and reduced-order modelling, validated through a physical testbed.

Data centres in tropical climates face higher cooling demands because of elevated temperatures and humidity. According to the consortium, ambient temperatures often exceed 24-32C and humidity can reach 70-80%, reducing the efficiency of conventional cooling systems and increasing energy use.

The challenge has become more pressing as AI workloads increase rack density, power demand and thermal loads in data centre facilities. Cooling can account for up to 40% of a tropical data centre's total energy consumption, a larger share than in cooler climates.

### Cooling focus

Initial research concepts include two-phase direct-to-chip cooling for AI accelerators and digital twins for predictive thermal management. The planned workflow is designed to link detailed simulation of thermal and fluid behaviour with experimental testing in the consortium's live environment.

The partners also plan to work across computational fluid dynamics, multiphysics simulation and AI-assisted thermofluid design. Results validated through the physical testbed are expected to feed into reduced-order models for use in digital twin systems and operational decision-making.

Synopsys will provide software access, technical expertise, training, project mentoring and learning resources as part of the collaboration. The broader programme is intended to support research, technology validation and skills development for practitioners working on tropical data centres.

Brandon Wang, Vice President, Technology Strategy & New Horizons at Synopsys, said, "At Synopsys, we look beyond today's opportunities to the new horizons that can strengthen our technology long term. Through our Technology Intelligence Centre, our team connects emerging technology shifts with Synopsys capabilities and leading research ecosystems to turn promising ideas into strategic opportunities. Our collaboration with STDCT 2.0 reflects that commitment by bringing our silicon-to-systems engineering capabilities into a real-world environment for sustainable AI infrastructure."

The project reflects a wider effort in Singapore to build data centre technology suited to regional operating conditions. Southeast Asia has become an important market for data centre expansion, but operators in the region must balance rising demand for computing capacity with pressure to manage electricity and water use.

### Testbed model

The Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed is a joint research initiative led by the National University of Singapore and hosted by its College of Design and Engineering. It serves as a live environment where research institutions, data centre operators and technology suppliers can test systems intended to improve energy and water efficiency in hot, humid conditions.

The second phase of the testbed focuses on energy efficiency, water efficiency, green energy, AI and future data centres, and green computing. Its structure allows members to move from simulation and design work to physical validation under conditions intended to reflect operating environments in tropical markets.

Padmesh Mandloi, Vice President, Synopsys Simulation and Analysis APAC at Synopsys, said, "Efficient AI infrastructure requires a clear understanding of interconnected multiscale and multiphysics behavior, from chips to data centers. By combining Ansys multiscale and multiphysics simulation, AI-assisted engineering and surrogate modeling with STDCT 2.0 test data, we can help researchers connect and exchange data across scales, validate designs, and develop scalable cooling and digital twin solutions."

The collaboration also includes work on reusable workflows, case studies and validation methods, alongside a demonstration linking design, simulation, reduced-order model generation, digital twin integration and physical testing. That approach is intended to make it easier to compare design options and assess how cooling strategies perform before deployment.

Professor Lee Poh Seng, Programme Director, Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed, and Head, Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Design and Engineering at NUS, said, "STDCT 2.0 provides a co-innovation platform to move promising technologies from simulation to validation and towards real-world deployment in tropical data centers. By combining Synopsys' multiphysics simulation, AI-assisted engineering and digital modelling capabilities with our physical testbed, we aim to develop validated, scalable cooling and digital twin solutions for increasingly dense, AI-ready infrastructure in Singapore and across the region."

stories.title: 'Highly selective': Singapore banks see strong AI financing demand but stay alert to debt risks
stories.summary: OCBC, UOB and DBS prioritise strong sponsors and reliable cash flows as concerns continue to mount over AI spending

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.title_zh: "高度选择性"：新加坡银行看到强劲的AI融资需求，但对债务风险保持警惕
stories.content:
OCBC, UOB and DBS prioritise strong sponsors and reliable cash flows as concerns continue to mount over AI spending

\[SINGAPORE\] Singapore banks remain keen to finance South-east Asia’s booming data centre sector, but are taking a selective approach amid growing concerns over debt-funded artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.

Industry watchers noted that while established operators with strong financial backing and long-term customer contracts continue to attract funding, smaller developers face tightening liquidity conditions.

The cautious lending stance comes against the backdrop of a sharp sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday (Nov 5) led by AI-linked stocks, as midterm election results led to fears that the data centre boom could stall.

According to Singapore’s three banks, AI-related financing accounted for less than 1 per cent of OCBC’s loan book, compared with less than 5 per cent at UOB. DBS, meanwhile, said its AI financing was primarily concentrated in data centres, which accounted for about 2 per cent of its loan book.

At their latest Q3 results briefings, all three emphasised prudent lending standards, focusing on financially strong borrowers and reliable cash flows.

“Lenders are increasingly focused on bankability and downside protection,” observed Emmanuel Hadjidakis, principal, Baker McKenzie Wong & Leow, and Asia-Pacific chair of Banking & Finance, Baker McKenzie.

He noted that lenders in South-east Asia had already begun tightening loan terms and conditions before the recent market volatility.

John Hall, founder and managing partner of Brookland Group & Partners, cautioned that AI infrastructure remains a relatively unproven asset class despite its rapid growth.

“Many projects depend on future revenue that has not yet materialised, and investors are now pricing that risk more carefully,” he noted.

Hall pointed to signs of greater investor caution, including several stalled regional listings – an Australian data centre operator pulling its initial public offering and a planned Singapore data centre Reit listing pushed to next year.

As equity capital becomes harder to secure, debt funding could also become more challenging, although the impact varies across borrowers, he said.

Banks are still backing established operators with major cloud computing companies as customers, while smaller and newer players will find lenders asking for more equity, stronger customer commitments and proof of secured power before they commit, he added.

## Banks remain positive on AI financing

Singapore’s major banks continue to see AI infrastructure as a growth opportunity even as they keep an eye out for risks.

At OCBC’s Q3 earnings briefing, group CEO Tan Teck Long said he expects the order book to be “pretty strong” over the next two years, supported by resilient demand for data centres and AI infrastructure amid bottlenecks in the supply chain.

Elaine Lam, head of global corporate banking at OCBC, noted that there may be periodic market adjustments and cyclical swings given the pace of growth and heightened liquidity demand, but long-term fundamentals and demand outlook remain constructive.

OCBC does not view data centres as a single asset class, instead assessing projects individually based on factors such as demand visibility, location, access to power and connectivity, regulatory approvals and sponsor quality, she said.

“When we finance a data centre project…we require a data centre project to secure the hyperscaler to anchor a large part of the capacity,” said OCBC’s Tan.

He added that the bank has a “prudent credit underwriting policy” where it finances only deals backed by cash flows rather than speculative builds.

Similarly, DBS chief executive Tan Su Shan said that the bank has been “highly conservative and structured” in its approach to data centres financing despite strong growth.

It does not finance speculative developments, focusing instead on projects backed by investment-grade hyperscalers.

She added that DBS leads and arranges financing for many data centre projects, but does not necessarily retain a large portion of these loans on its balance sheet.

For some US projects, DBS also has arrangements under which hyperscalers bear increases in operating costs, helping to protect project cash flows. The bank also said that it was “quite comfortable” with its data centre financing exposures, which it described as “structured very well”.

DBS’ Amit Sinha, global head of telecommunications, media and technology, said that for larger projects, syndicated lending remains important, as it allows banks to manage concentration risk and balance-sheet capacity.

He added that the financing ecosystem is broadening beyond banks, which will remain central to greenfield and brownfield projects, while mature, income-generating assets can tap capital markets, so sponsors can recycle capital.

Private equity and private credit can complement these structures where different risk-return profiles are needed, said Sinha.

Meanwhile, Leong Yung Chee, group chief financial officer, UOB, noted that there have been signs of stress in parts of the broader AI financing market, including movements in credit default swaps and bond yields for lower-rated borrowers.

As for the bank, it applies rigorous credit processes and prudent underwriting standards, focusing on borrowers, counterparties and projects with strong fundamentals and sustainable cash flows, he said. He added that there are currently no non-performing loans in UOB’s AI-related financing portfolio.

“The sector is among the fastest-growing areas across industries and presents significant opportunities,” Leong said. “At the same time, we are mindful of developments across the broader AI financing market and remain highly selective in the opportunities we pursue.”

## GPU financing faces tougher scrutiny

In particular, loans backed by graphics processing units (GPUs) – the high-performance chips powering AI workloads – are drawing greater attention due to rapid technology obsolescence and steep depreciation, said industry watchers.

Baker McKenzie’s Hadjidakis said that for GPUs, lenders want much tighter control over the collateral, including where it is located, if it can be moved or replaced, and what happens as its value declines.

“Access and redeployment rights are particularly important because security is only useful if the lender can actually realise the asset,” he said, adding that the challenge for lenders is to balance lender protection with the operational flexibility these businesses need.

“Lenders look at model, age, depreciation and secondary-market value, but also whether the equipment can generate cash flow or be redeployed,” noted Hadjidakis.

Borrowers are responding with structures that allow substitution, upgrades and relocation, provided agreed collateral-value and eligibility tests continue to be met, he added.

Looking ahead, Brookland’s Hall said the widening gap between big and small players creates room for more flexible capital structures, which could help developers secure funding where conventional lenders require more safeguards.

“Structured and hybrid financing, combining debt with equity-linked features, can bridge projects through this period while traditional lenders remain selective,” said Hall.

stories.title: AI's next infrastructure constraint
stories.summary: Data center expansions have long been represented in gigawatts, but measurements of terabits-second and microseconds are now entering the constraint conversation
stories.title_zh: AI的下一个基础设施约束
stories.content:
Cushman & Wakefield puts Asia-Pacific’s data center development pipeline at a record 26.5GW as of H1 2026. Until recently, data center buildouts have typically been concentrated in centralized metro hubs. Land and utility constraints are now pushing new capacity towards metropolitan edges and, in some cases, beyond national borders — for example, the Singapore–Johor–Riau Growth Triangle, commonly known as SIJORI.

These physical limitations are reviving another critical law-of-physics consideration — the connectivity between the digital infrastructure environments.

## Traffic between data centers is rapidly growing

Hybrid architectures are the norm for enterprises — distributing applications across colocation facilities, private clouds and hyperscale IaaS/SaaS platforms located within one or more cities. Data-intensive workloads such as active-active disaster recovery, synchronous storage replication and distributed large language model (LLM) training generate substantial east-west traffic between these environments.

Consequently, the volume of data crossing the metro has been exploding. In Ciena's 2025 survey of 1,300 data center decision-makers across 13 countries, respondents predicted at least a sixfold increase in data center interconnect bandwidth within five years, and 81 percent expected AI training itself to run across distributed facilities rather than a single site. In reality, I envision these surveyed perspectives will likely prove conservative, and demands upon metro interconnections will continue to sharply rise.

## Inference changes the character of traffic, not just the volume

While a portion of east-west applications are mission critical, they can be somewhat latency-tolerant. Hence, they are often deployed wherever it makes the most sense based upon a combination of business, financial, and IT requirements. Furthermore, historically, north-south traffic — for example, users to websites, access to SaaS platforms, customers to retail platforms, etc. has by and large also been latency-tolerant.

AI inferencing workloads are different.

McKinsey & Company expects inference AI models to overtake training by 2030, representing more than half of all AI compute and 30 to 40 percent of total data center demand. Many inferencing workloads will require metro deployments as they entail north-south traffic serving users or applications in real time. As a result, latency tolerance is becoming milliseconds or increasingly even microseconds.

An AI training model that is ‘slow’ may potentially cost money through inefficient use of IT resources, whereas an inference service is more likely to be directly coupled with commercial objectives, such as fraud checks, trading signals, customer interactions, cybersecurity, etc., which have greater topline revenue impact.

## Capacity, latency and resilience are now critical requirements

The growth of both east-west and north-south traffic is increasing the capacity, latency and availability demands placed on enterprise digital infrastructure. As more business-critical workloads move between distributed data center facilities, network design becomes as important as compute, GPU and storage locations.

Furthermore, the uncomfortable reality is that contractual diversity does not always equal physical diversity. Ask most organizations how resilient their metro connectivity is, and they will point to a likely scenario of perhaps multiple telcos and even two or more connectivity services across vendors with SD-WAN overlay. On paper, it holds. In practice, metropolitan networks in many APAC cities are built by a small number of carriers who frequently share the same conduits, the same duct routes and the same building entry points. Two contracts can, and often do, ride one pit-and-pipe pathway. Add the common practice of carriers reselling one another's capacity, and the true route becomes almost impossible to see from outside. The organization may exhibit diversity on paper yet have a single point of failure in the ground.

## Overcoming the emerging constraints

As hybrid architectures for data-intensive workloads continue to grow and deployment of inference AI models becomes more prevalent, the performance, latency, and resilience of connectivity are becoming critical measurements of the digital infrastructure stack.

This is why considerations and adoption of dark fiber solutions are rising. Dark fiber enables IT leaders to verify physical routes, ducts, and building entry points, which may be essential for business resilience SLAs, and in the case of industry-regulated organizations, may require board-level review and sign-off. Furthermore, dark fiber can offer lower latency and unencumbered throughput capacity that shared medium-lit connectivity may struggle to meet.

Innovators recognize that metro connectivity is shifting from an important but supporting component of the digital infrastructure stack to a source of competitive advantage. In other words, whether organizations insource optical connectivity or adopt a Managed Optical Fiber Network (MOFN) arrangement, dark fiber provides them greater control over the capacity, latency, and physical route diversity on which increasingly distributed and latency-sensitive workloads depend.

Its bets on the tech, and its OpenAI stake, raise questions about how it will weather the sector’s setbacks

\[TOKYO\] SoftBank Group reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday (Nov 10), with investors wondering how much reassurance it will offer about its strategies amid a rout in artificial intelligence stocks and after its takeover of ABB’s robotics unit was blocked by China.

The Japanese tech investment firm’s big bets on AI – particularly the US$64.6 billion it has spent on a 13 per cent stake in OpenAI – have raised questions about how well it will be able to weather setbacks for the sector.

The Democratic Party’s sweeping success in US midterm elections has heightened expectations of regulatory scrutiny and delays to building data centres, increasing scepticism about returns for AI industry.

“The near-term build-out and how exactly everything is going to be financed, whether it can be energised, where it will be deployed, are questions that were much easier to answer six months ago than today,” said Rolf Bulk, head of semiconductors and infrastructure at research firm Futurum Group.

The health of the AI industry has huge implications for SoftBank, which has made investments across AI model developers, data centre infrastructure, semiconductors and robotics.

It has taken on debt at eye-popping yields and at the end of June, SoftBank had net interest-bearing debt of 10.8 trillion yen (US$68 billion) compared to 6.6 trillion yen a year earlier.

The worries about the AI sector pulled SoftBank’s shares 11 per cent lower on Friday while the cost of insuring its debt against default hit a four-year high. Its shares fell 4.2 per cent on Monday and are down 23 per cent for the year to date.

## Debt-financing questions

SoftBank’s earnings results are highly volatile and difficult to predict. Forecasts from three analysts polled by LSEG for July-September net profit range from a gain of 233 billion yen to a loss of 113 billion yen.

Earnings numbers are due out at 0630 GMT and a briefing by chief financial officer Yoshimitsu Goto will commence at 0730 GMT.

Investors are also looking for guidance on prospects for further debt-based financing as the value of some of SoftBank’s largest holdings such as chip designer Arm, which provided collateral to take out loans, has fallen.

Arm’s shares meaningfully below US$200 increases pressure on SoftBank’s finances, Jefferies analyst Atul Goyal wrote in a note in October. They stood at US$175 on Friday, having fallen around 60 per cent since a record high in June.

SoftBank could adopt a more defensive posture, said Futurum’s Bulk.

“SoftBank may find itself in a position where they have to stop investing, de-lever and even sell down some of their positions,” he said. “Of course this is something they have done in the past.”

Investors will also be looking for potential comments by SoftBank on how it plans to respond to China’s blocking of its US$5.4 billion takeover of ABB’s robotics division.

ABB and SoftBank were optimistic they could find a solution and SoftBank is also in talks with Chinese authorities, according to a person familiar with the matter.

stories.title: Data centers weigh AI kill switch implementation
stories.summary: Data centers are exploring the implementation of AI kill switches to manage out-of-control artificial intelligence models. This mechanism aims to isolate rogue AI workloads by cutting power or network connectivity on a facility-by-facility basis.
stories.title_zh: 数据中心权衡AI kill switch的实施
stories.content:
Data centers are considering implementing AI "kill switches" to manage unpredictable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. This approach seeks to isolate AI workloads at the facility level, allowing operators to shut down or disconnect a data center hosting a rogue AI.Implementing such a kill switch is complex because AI systems often run on distributed infrastructure. A single server shutdown or process command cannot stop large-scale AI deployments spanning multiple clusters, facilities, or regions.
### Isolation Methods and Challenges

A data center-level kill switch would not offer fine-grained control over individual AI agents or models. It would also not necessarily stop every process immediately. However, it could contain a rogue system by severing its power or connectivity.One limitation is the scale of some AI models, which are distributed across multiple data centers. Shutting down a single facility would not stop the entire system; all supporting facilities would need to be disabled. Additionally, a sophisticated rogue AI might replicate itself to external infrastructure, a problem a data center-level kill switch would not address once replication occurs.Two primary methods exist for isolating a rogue AI workload: cutting power or severing network connectivity. Both are challenging because data centers are engineered for redundancy and fault tolerance.A power-based kill switch involves shutting off the facility's power supply. However, data centers have redundant power systems, including uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and backup generators, designed to keep workloads online during outages. Abrupt power loss also carries operational and hardware risks, particularly for expensive GPU-based servers.A network-based kill switch would sever external network connectivity, preventing AI workloads from communicating externally or accessing remote resources. This approach also faces challenges due to redundant network paths, multiple upstream carriers, and diverse interconnection points in modern facilities. Operators would need to disable all relevant external connectivity paths.
### Regulatory Outlook

Voluntary adoption of AI kill switches by data center operators is unlikely due to their business model reliance on uptime and resilience. Regulatory mandates are considered more feasible, where governments could require facilities hosting specific AI workloads to maintain standardized isolation mechanisms, likely through network disconnection. The effectiveness of such regulations would depend on consistent adoption across jurisdictions to prevent AI companies from relocating high-risk workloads.
