SYDNEY (Nov 9): Australian data centre operator NextDC said on Monday that it would stop work on all projects without customer contracts following a big setback on a facility in Melbourne, as two major rivals finalised buying an A$715 million (US$492 million) stake in the company.

A suspension of work on its flagship M3 data centre expansion in Melbourne due to power delays and community backlash forced the company to cut its earnings forecasts last month, sending its share price tumbling 42%.

The decision to pause uncontracted projects after the Melbourne delay is another blow for NextDC, which had been touted as Australia's most prolific data centre developer.

"The last couple of weeks (I) certainly didn't expect to be in the position we're in today having to deal with some delays," NextDC's chief executive Craig Scroggie told the UBS Australasia conference.

"That's unfortunately probably reflective of the global environment in relation to the engagement, social licence, people's feelings about artificial intelligence and data centres being the physical embodiment of that."

Scroggie said the M3 delay meant the top priority was to win community backing for that project and "anything that didn't have a customer contract and a customer commitment that we absolutely have to deliver on is now no longer a priority".

He did not say how many projects would be paused. The company had 11 centres in development or in the planning stages, according to its 2026 annual report.

"That work can't restart until we clearly communicate that we've solved this problem, that we've earned the trust of everybody that's been supporting us, and then we will get back to work."

NextDC's rivals Goodman Group and its New York-listed partner Digital Realty bought a 9.9% stake in the company last week, following the share price plunge.

"When you have a challenge like we've had in the last couple of weeks, it's not really any surprise to me that people ... look at that and say, now might be the time," Scroggie said.

Goodman and Digital Realty said they had no plans at the moment to launch a takeover offer, but reserved the right to do so. They said they would "look forward to a potential collaboration with the NextDC board and management on the ways and forms in which the parties may help to address the challenges facing the company".

Following their share raid, NextDC's share price recovered the ground lost from the earnings writedown.

stories.content:
The startup is staking claim to the industry’s next frontier of agentic infrastructure

\[BENGALURU\] DeepSeek, the Chinese artificial intelligence disruptor, released striking adoption numbers for its AI agent infrastructure as it continues to challenge Anthropic and OpenAI with an entire swath of applications built around open-source AI technologies.

On Sunday (Nov 8), the Hangzhou-headquartered startup disclosed on X that DeepSeek Harness, its open-source agent application, had reached 1.54 million daily active users by Wednesday (Nov 4), less than three months after its Aug 13 debut.

Daily users were at about 271,000 at the end of September, right after it released a desktop version of the app, based on the number of users connecting to its own servers.

DeepSeek, which jolted Silicon Valley with its low-cost reasoning model R1 in 2025, is staking claim to the next frontier of the industry: infrastructure for AI agents, software that lets AI act autonomously on a user’s behalf.

DeepSeek is planning an official marketplace where developers can publish plug-ins and users can discover them.

It is also planning a support programme for plug-in creators including token grants, technical assistance and promotional opportunities. No further details have been disclosed.

The new moves reflect a broader shift in the AI industry where the battle for users is increasingly being fought over ecosystems and integration rather than model performance.

DeepSeek is positioning Harness as an open, developer-driven agent ecosystem to challenge OpenAI and Anthropic not just on model performance and cost, but on the breadth of applications built around its AI technology.

The AI disruptor is betting that third-party applications and specialised tools will build traction around its open-source AI agent infrastructure and become a decisive source of competitive advantage against Silicon Valley’s proprietary technologies, as the AI industry moves beyond chatbots towards autonomous agents.

AI agents carry out multi-step tasks on behalf of the user such as writing and modifying code, analysing files, conducting research and using other tools with minimal human supervision.

Harness’ appetite for computational power is notable.

The application is consuming approximately 92 trillion tokens daily, which works out to about 60 million tokens daily for each active user – providing among the first available evidence of AI agents steeply escalating the demand for processing power.

The scale shows that the hunger for compute power in AI agents is vastly higher than that of chatbots, as AI agents run for multiple hours as they read or write code, use other tools and go on the web, all with little human intervention.

The startup is building Harness as a “everything is a plug-in” architecture.

A plug-in adds a special feature to a piece of software without changing it, giving it added functionality. DeepSeek counts about 35,000 plug-ins and 60 per cent of users have built at least one of them, though the startup said that the sophistication of the plug-ins varies. BLOOMBERG
